channel.title: Automation on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Automation on Best of AI

item.title: 11x
item.description:
11x’s pitch is that AI can do the work of a sales development representative. Alice researches prospects, writes personalized outreach, sends messages across email and LinkedIn, and tries to book meetings. A voice agent, Julian, makes phone calls and follows up. The company presents them as digital workers that run around the clock.

Customers connect their CRM and define the audience and message guidelines, and the agents work through lead lists and hand interested prospects to human salespeople. The approach can raise the volume of outreach well beyond what a small team could do by hand, though response quality depends on targeting and data.

item.title: Adobe Firefly AI Assistant
item.description: Firefly AI Assistant is Adobe’s attempt to bring an agent into its creative apps. Instead of opening each application and applying tools by hand, you describe an outcome, such as adapting a campaign image into several social formats or preparing a video with captions, and the assistant works out the steps. It then carries them out across the right apps in order. The project began under the name Project Moonlight before launching as Firefly AI Assistant.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.description: AgentCore addresses the infrastructure work of taking an agent from prototype to production. A runtime hosts agents with session isolation so each user’s work is kept separate, and handles scaling. Identity features let agents authenticate to other services on a user’s behalf, a gateway turns existing APIs and services into tools agents can call, and observability traces what agents do. Developers can use it with frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, and the Strands Agents SDK, and with models on Bedrock or from other providers.

item.title: Azure AI Foundry
item.description: Foundry is where Microsoft brings together its AI development tools for businesses. A catalog lists models from OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, and others, which you can test side by side and deploy through one set of APIs. Everything runs under Azure’s identity, networking, and compliance controls, which is what many regulated companies need before they can use generative AI. The service has gone through several names, including Azure AI Studio, so older tutorials may use different labels.

item.title: BabyAGI
item.description:
BabyAGI arrived early in the wave of autonomous agent experiments. The original script was only a few dozen lines: given an objective, a language model creates a task list, executes the first task, stores the result in a vector database, then generates and reprioritizes new tasks based on what it learned. That simple loop was widely copied and adapted.

The project mattered because it made the idea of an AI agent easy to understand and try. It sparked many descendants and discussion about what autonomous systems could do, and developers learned from its limits, such as loops, drift, and cost. Later versions were reworked into a framework for building self-improving agents with functions stored in a database.

item.title: Bardeen
item.description:
Bardeen automates repetitive work that happens on web pages. A user installs the extension, then runs playbooks that click through sites, extract data, and send it elsewhere. Typical uses include scraping lists of people from LinkedIn into Google Sheets, saving a company’s details to a CRM, or sending a meeting summary to Slack.

A natural language builder lets users describe what they want, and the AI assembles the steps, which can be edited. Triggers run automations on a schedule or when something happens, and integrations cover hundreds of apps. Sales and recruiting teams, who spend time moving data between tabs, are heavy users.

item.title: Baserow
item.description:
Baserow gives teams an easy way to build databases. It looks like a spreadsheet, but tables can link to each other, store different field types, and show data as a grid, gallery, kanban board, calendar, or form. People without coding skills build trackers, inventories, and small internal tools with it.

It is open source, so companies can run it on their own servers, which appeals to those with data residency or privacy needs. The platform has a REST API and webhooks, an application builder for interfaces, and automations that run on triggers. An AI assistant can create tables from a prompt, and AI fields can generate or classify values for each row.

item.title: Boomi
item.description:
Boomi was one of the first cloud integration platforms. Its visual builder lets teams connect applications and move data between them, with a large catalog of connectors, API management, data integration, and workflow automation in one platform. Companies use it to sync records between sales, finance, HR, and operations systems without extensive custom code.

The company has leaned into AI agents. Boomi lets teams build agents that use connected systems as tools, and offers an agent catalog and controls to track what agents are allowed to do, which matters as companies deploy many of them. Data management and master data tools help keep records consistent across systems.

item.title: Claude Cowork
item.description: Cowork takes the agent approach behind Claude Code and puts it in an ordinary app window. Instead of typing commands, you describe a job such as sorting a folder of receipts, turning notes into a report, or building a spreadsheet from several PDFs. Claude breaks the request into steps, makes a plan, works on the files you have shared with it, and reports back when it finishes. Files it reads or creates appear in a panel so you can open them.

item.title: Databricks Agent Bricks
item.description: Agent Bricks is aimed at companies that want agents grounded in their own data. Rather than writing everything by hand, a team describes the task, such as answering questions over internal documents, extracting information from forms, or coordinating several agents, and the platform helps build it. It generates synthetic test data, evaluates quality with judges, and tunes the agent by trying different models and settings to improve accuracy and cost.

item.title: Figma Weave
item.description: Weave brings generative image workflows into Figma. Instead of exporting an image to another tool, a designer can run a prebuilt workflow on a selected layer, for example swapping the background of a product shot, applying an artistic style to an image, or creating variations. More than twenty such workflows cover common creative tasks, and the results land back in the design file, ready to be used in a layout.

item.title: Gemini Spark
item.description:
Spark is Google’s move toward an always-on assistant. You give it jobs, such as pulling together information from your inbox and documents, preparing for a trip, or following up on a task over several days, and it works in the background on dedicated virtual machines in Google’s cloud. Because it runs there, it keeps going even when your phone or laptop is off, and it reports back with results.

Control is part of the design. Spark asks for permission before taking significant actions such as sending messages or making purchases, and users can set skills and schedules to automate recurring work. It starts with Gmail, Docs, and other Google services, and connects to outside tools through the Model Context Protocol and integrations. On Android, a running agent’s progress is meant to be visible at the top of the screen.

item.title: GitHub Agent HQ
item.description: Agent HQ is GitHub’s way of treating coding agents as a team you manage instead of a single assistant. Rather than choosing one AI vendor, a developer can assign work to agents from different providers, such as OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code, from the same place where code, issues, and pull requests already live. Each agent works on its task and returns changes for review in the usual pull request flow.

item.title: IBM Bob
item.description:
Bob is IBM’s agentic assistant for software development. Instead of only autocompleting code, it takes part in the full lifecycle: understanding a codebase, planning changes, writing and reviewing code, generating tests, and helping with deployment. Different agents take on roles, such as architect or reviewer, and work inside the developer’s editor.

Enterprise use is the focus. IBM emphasizes security and governance, with protection against sensitive data leaks, policy enforcement, and testing of the AI for vulnerabilities. It routes tasks among several language models, including IBM’s own Granite family and models from other providers, and is positioned for modernization work such as moving older Java or COBOL applications.

item.title: LangGraph
item.description:
LangGraph models an agent as a graph. Each node is a step, such as calling a model, running a tool, or checking a condition, and edges define the flow between steps, including loops and branches. A shared state object passes information along. This explicit structure gives developers control over what the agent does and when, which makes complex agents easier to reason about than a free-running loop.

Features aimed at production use set it apart. Checkpointing saves state so a run can pause and resume, or recover from failure. Human-in-the-loop steps let an agent wait for approval before taking an action, and time-travel debugging lets developers replay and edit earlier steps. It supports streaming of intermediate results, long-term memory, and multi-agent designs, in Python and JavaScript.

item.title: Microsoft Copilot Studio
item.description:
Copilot Studio lets organizations create their own AI agents without heavy coding. In a visual editor, makers describe an agent’s purpose, connect knowledge sources such as SharePoint sites and websites, add topics and actions, and test it in a chat window. The finished agent can be published to Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, websites, and messaging channels, and can answer questions, complete tasks, or hand off to people.

Its strength is connection to business systems. Hundreds of connectors reach tools like Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, and Dynamics 365, and agents can use Power Automate flows to run processes. Autonomous agents can respond to triggers such as a new email or record, not only a chat message, and the platform supports the Model Context Protocol to reach more tools. Administrators manage governance, data loss prevention, and access through Microsoft’s admin centers.

item.title: Mistral Vibe
item.description:
Vibe is Mistral’s agent for software work. The command-line version runs in a project directory, reads and writes files, searches code, runs shell commands, and tracks tasks, using Mistral’s coding models to carry out requests such as fixing bugs, adding features, and explaining code. It is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, written in Python, and integrates with editors such as Zed and with other tools.

The broader Vibe offering extends agent capabilities to office tasks and teams. It builds on Mistral’s Devstral coding models and its large general models, which are available through Mistral’s API and, for some, as open weights that organizations can run on their own servers. This flexibility is a selling point for companies and governments that want agents without relying on US cloud providers.

item.title: NemoClaw
item.description:
OpenClaw is an open-source agent project that can carry out tasks on a user’s computer and accounts, which made it popular and also raised security worries. NemoClaw is NVIDIA’s response for organizations: it installs OpenClaw inside an isolated runtime, called OpenShell, with strict default permissions, so the agent can only touch what administrators allow. A privacy router helps decide which requests can use outside models and which stay local.

NVIDIA pairs the platform with its Nemotron models and with its NeMo software for building and managing agents, but says NemoClaw works on different hardware and with other models. It was announced with a group of enterprise partners and early integrations with agent frameworks, positioning NVIDIA to offer software as well as chips for the agent era.

item.title: NocoDB
item.description:
NocoDB turns a database into something that feels like Airtable. Connect it to an existing SQL database or create a new one, and users see tables as spreadsheets they can filter, sort, and edit, with views as kanban boards, galleries, calendars, and forms. Non-technical colleagues get access to data without learning SQL.

It generates REST and GraphQL APIs for tables, supports permissions and webhooks, and offers automation and an AI assistant to help with fields and queries. Because it is open source, teams can host it themselves and keep data on their own servers.

item.title: Notion Custom Agents
item.description: Custom Agents extend Notion AI from something you chat with into something that works on its own. A team sets up an agent with instructions and the content it can access, then chooses what should trigger it: a schedule, a comment on a page, a change to a database, an @mention, or messages in a public Slack channel. The agent then does the job, such as triaging incoming requests, compiling a weekly report, updating a tracker, or answering questions in a channel.

item.title: Perplexity Computer
item.description: Perplexity Computer extends Perplexity from answering questions to doing work. You give it a goal, such as researching a market and building a report, tracking a set of sources, or assembling a presentation, and it plans the job, splits it into parts, and runs them, sometimes in parallel. Different steps are sent to different AI models depending on what they are good at, which is the central idea of the product.

item.title: Replit Agent 4
item.description: Replit Agent 4 continues the idea that you can describe software and have an agent build it. In the Replit workspace, you explain what you want, and the agent writes the code, sets up the environment and database, tests the result, and deploys it. You review progress, give feedback in plain language, and ask for changes. Replit says this version is substantially faster than its predecessor, which matters because building an app involves many steps.

item.title: Salesforce Agentforce
item.description: Agentforce lets companies deploy AI agents that work inside Salesforce. An agent might answer customer questions, qualify inbound leads, schedule meetings, or update records, using the company’s own data and rules. Builders define an agent’s role, topics, and the actions it may take, connect it to knowledge and data, and test it before release. A reasoning engine decides how to handle each request, and guardrails limit what the agent may do.

item.title: SAP Joule
item.description:
Joule is the assistant inside SAP’s software. Instead of navigating menus in an ERP, finance, or HR system, users ask questions such as which invoices are overdue or what the status of an order is, and Joule retrieves the answer from live business data. It respects the user’s permissions, so it only shows what that person is allowed to see.

It has grown from a question-and-answer helper into a platform for agents. Prebuilt Joule agents handle tasks like processing invoices or supporting recruiters, and Joule Studio lets customers and partners build their own agents and skills that work across SAP and non-SAP systems. SAP presents this as part of a broader business AI platform that connects data and models.

item.title: SAP Signavio
item.description:
Signavio helps companies understand how their processes really work. Teams model processes in a visual notation so everyone can see the intended steps, owners, and rules, and store them in a shared repository. This makes it easier to document, improve, and standardize work across departments.

Process mining adds evidence. By reading event logs from systems like SAP ERP, it reconstructs what happened in practice, revealing delays, rework, and variants that differ from the designed flow. Analysts can then quantify the impact and decide what to fix. Collaboration and journey modeling tools help teams plan transformations such as moving to a new ERP.

item.title: ServiceNow Otto
item.description:
Otto is ServiceNow’s way of unifying its AI products into a single assistant. It combines the conversational search that came from Moveworks, the workflow skills of Now Assist, and an agentic interface on the Now Platform. An employee can ask for help in plain language, and Otto finds an answer or starts the workflow that does the job, such as requesting access or opening an IT ticket.

The point is action across systems. ServiceNow positions it as an assistant that works with the enterprise tools a person already uses, not just answering from a knowledge base. Governance is a major theme: AI Control Tower tracks the agents, logs interactions, and enforces policies, which matters when many agents are acting at once.

item.title: Slackbot
item.description:
Slackbot used to be a simple helper that answered canned questions. It has been rebuilt as an agent that works across a Slack workspace. You can ask it to find a decision made in a channel, summarize a thread, draft a message or a document, schedule a meeting from calendar availability, or pull together information from several conversations, and it answers using content you already have permission to see.

Beyond answering, it can take actions. Slackbot can post, set reminders, update records through connected apps, and delegate longer tasks to agents built with Salesforce’s Agentforce, tying Slack more closely to the rest of Salesforce’s platform. Slack has used models from partners to power it, and the assistant adapts to the user’s context and role within the workspace.

item.title: Stripe Agentic Commerce Suite
item.description:
As AI agents begin to shop and pay on behalf of people, merchants and payment systems need a way to handle it. Stripe’s suite helps businesses become discoverable to agents: a merchant uploads a product catalog, chooses which agent platforms to sell through, and Stripe handles discovery, checkout, and payments.

It builds on open protocols. The Agentic Commerce Protocol, developed with OpenAI, defines how an agent and a merchant negotiate a checkout. The Machine Payments Protocol, written with Tempo, lets agents and services coordinate payments in code, including small recurring transactions. Stripe also supports an agent wallet and stablecoin payments over the x402 protocol, and it issues limited-use tokens so an agent can spend within set limits.

item.title: SuperAGI
item.description:
SuperAGI appeared during the first wave of autonomous agent interest. It offered a framework and dashboard for creating agents that use tools, with features for running several agents at once, managing resources, and viewing performance.

The company later built applications on top of the framework for sales and marketing automation. Many agent frameworks have emerged since, and the field has moved toward different designs and commercial platforms.

SuperAGI is open source, with paid products. Check its repository for current activity. Alternatives include LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Dify. SuperAGI suits developers who want to explore an open agent platform.

item.title: Twilio ConversationRelay
item.description:
ConversationRelay connects phone calls to AI. When a call arrives on a Twilio number, the service converts the caller’s speech to text in real time and streams it over a WebSocket to the developer’s server. The server sends text back, which Twilio converts into speech, so the caller hears a natural response. This lets teams plug in any large language model and their own business logic.

Twilio manages the hard parts of voice. It handles interruptions when a caller speaks over the agent, supports multiple languages and voice providers, and can transfer the call to a human with the transcript. It also offers a no-code Studio widget for simpler flows, plus compliance support for regulated industries, including options for HIPAA and PCI. A reporting feature gives insight into latency and where agents struggle.

item.title: Zapier MCP
item.description:
Zapier MCP turns Zapier’s app library into tools an AI can use. You create an MCP server, choose the apps and actions you want to allow, such as sending a Slack message, adding a row in Google Sheets, or creating a CRM contact, and connect that server to a compatible client. The assistant can then call those actions during a conversation.

This avoids writing custom integrations. Zapier already handles authentication and the quirks of each app’s API, so connecting an assistant to a new service is a matter of adding an action and authorizing your account. You control the scope, and each call uses your connected account, which helps limit what the AI can touch.

item.title: beacon.sh
item.description:
beacon.sh addresses a limit of coding agents: they start each session knowing little about the project. Beacon watches what the agent does, such as commands that work, mistakes it makes, and conventions it discovers, and stores them as notes the agent can use next time.

It works with popular coding agents and keeps the memory in files and a local store the developer can inspect and edit. Over time, that cuts repeated explanations and failed attempts.

item.title: Cedric
item.description:
Cedric acts as a stand-in for meetings. A user gives it slides, notes, and background documents, and it attends a call, presents, and responds to questions using that material. When it does not know something, it can note the question for follow-up.

The idea appeals to people with a heavy meeting load, such as founders or sales teams running repeated demos. It raises etiquette and trust questions: others in the meeting should know they are talking to an AI agent.

item.title: ClawsGO Science
item.description:
ClawsGO Science goes beyond literature review. The agent can plan an analysis, write and run code in a cloud environment, process datasets, and report results with the steps shown. It is built for scientific work such as data analysis and computational experiments.

Doing the work, not only describing it, can speed up exploratory research. Results still need scrutiny, since an agent can make statistical or coding mistakes, and reproducibility depends on seeing exactly what was run.

item.title: UnleashX
item.description:
UnleashX provides voice and workflow automation. Teams configure AI agents that handle phone conversations and carry out actions across systems, such as calling leads, qualifying them, updating records, and sending follow-ups. Rules define what the worker may do.

The platform presents these as digital employees for roles like sales development and support. Outbound calling needs consent and compliance with telemarketing rules, and AI voice agents should disclose themselves.

UnleashX is paid, and independent information is limited, so run a pilot first. Alternatives include Bland AI, Retell AI, Vapi, Synthflow, and 11x. UnleashX suits small teams automating calls and follow-ups.

item.title: DeepSeek Super-Agent
item.description:
Super-Agent explores what a team-facing coding agent could look like. Built on DeepSeek’s Harness runtime, it is tied to one GitHub repository and listens for requests from approved colleagues in Feishu, a workplace chat app. A teammate can ask it to investigate or change something, and it works on the code and reports back.

The prototype shows how a lab thinks about agents inside everyday collaboration tools instead of only in a developer’s terminal. Because it is a prototype, it focuses on demonstrating the design, not on a polished product with broad integrations, and it requires technical setup.

item.title: Herdr
item.description:
Herdr manages the growing pile of agent sessions developers run. Instead of many terminal windows, it presents agents in one tabbed interface and shows whether each is working, finished, or waiting for input, when the agent reports status. It supports any agent that runs in a terminal.

The key design choice is the herdr-core runtime, a small server on your machine that runs the sessions. The app is only a front end, so quitting or updating it does not stop agents. A terminal version of Herdr, the original, still exists as a separate program with its own server.

item.title: Claude Duet
item.description: Duet is built on the idea that an assistant should not wait for you to ask. Each morning it sends a brief on what matters across your connected apps, and it checks those accounts every few hours for new items that need attention. You can hand it tasks, and it works on its own virtual machine with a browser, so your laptop or phone does not need to stay on. It keeps working while you are away and tells you when something is done or needs a decision.

item.title: Conduyt
item.description:
Conduyt takes an approach to CRM pricing that departs from the per-seat model. A team pays a single price no matter how many people use the product, which suits small sales teams and agencies that would otherwise pay for every added user.

The basics are familiar: a contact database, deal pipelines, and activity tracking, with AI features that draft follow-up messages, summarize interactions, and reduce routine data entry. Positioned as AI-native, it aims to have the software do the admin work that salespeople dislike.

item.title: Celonis
item.description:
Celonis is the best-known process mining platform. Every action in business systems, such as creating an order or approving an invoice, leaves a record with a time stamp. Celonis reads these logs and rebuilds the real process, showing the paths that cases take, where they wait, and how often they deviate from the intended flow.

With that picture, teams find delays, rework, and costly exceptions. The platform quantifies the impact, suggests improvements, and can trigger automated actions or alerts. AI features answer questions about process data and recommend where to focus. Common uses include order-to-cash, procure-to-pay, and supply chain work.

item.title: OpenAI Dots
item.description: Dots move ChatGPT from a tool you open to an assistant that keeps working. Each dot has its own cloud computer with a browser, so it can carry out tasks on websites and in apps without tying up your device. You give it goals, such as keeping track of your inbox, preparing for meetings, or monitoring a project, and it works in the background, checking back when it needs input. Over time it learns from your feedback.

item.title: Grok Bot
item.description:
Grok Bot takes a different shape from a chat window. A user creates named bots and assigns them tasks, and each bot runs in the cloud, keeps working after the user closes their laptop, and can sign into apps and use a browser to complete work. Examples include handling inbox tasks, researching topics, and running routine workflows.

The product emphasizes persistence. Bots remember context over time and report back, and the cloud computer gives them a place to store files and run tools. It is positioned for both individuals and businesses, with a business version aimed at agents that log into company applications.

item.title: Sider Omni Sidebar
item.description:
Sider began as a browser sidebar for chatting with AI about web pages. Omni Sidebar extends the idea to the whole Mac: a panel that sees the content in the active app and lets users ask questions, summarize, draft replies, or take actions without copying and pasting.

The assistant supports several underlying models and can work with files and screenshots. For people who live in email, documents, and spreadsheets, an assistant that sees the same screen saves steps.

item.title: Meta Muse
item.description: Muse is Meta’s step from a chat assistant to an agent that acts on your behalf. You ask it to do something, such as arrange a trip, draft and send an email, or handle a multi-step errand, and it works across apps and websites to complete the job. Each user’s agent runs in a secure virtual machine, so it can continue working after you leave the app and come back when it needs a decision.

item.title: MagiCrew
item.description:
MagiCrew packages agent capabilities in one open-source system. A general agent can plan and complete tasks with tools, a visual workflow editor lets users build repeatable processes, and messaging and collaboration features let teams work with agents in shared spaces.

Because it is open source, organizations can host it themselves and adapt it, which appeals to teams with privacy requirements or specific needs. It extends an existing open-source project, which gives it a base of users and code to build on.

item.title: ChatGPT Atlas
item.description:
Atlas puts ChatGPT inside the browser. A sidebar assistant can see the page you are on, so you can ask it to summarize an article, explain a table, compare products across tabs, or draft a reply in context. The address bar can also act as a chat prompt, and the browser can remember context from your browsing if you turn that on.

Agent mode goes further. The assistant can take actions on your behalf, such as navigating to a site, filling in a form, or doing research across several pages, while you watch and can take over. This capability is powerful and also risky, since web pages can contain instructions meant to trick an agent, a problem known as prompt injection.

item.title: Viktor
item.description:
Viktor lives where teams already talk. Instead of a separate app, a colleague mentions Viktor in a channel and asks for something, such as pulling numbers from a dashboard, building a report, or writing a script, and it replies in the thread. It watches how the team works and picks up context over time.

It connects to a very large number of business tools, so it can read from and act in systems like CRMs, analytics, and ad platforms, and it can produce artifacts such as documents and simple web apps. Skills can be added for specialized work.

item.title: Comet
item.description:
Comet makes the assistant part of the browser. Instead of copying content into a chatbot, users can ask questions about the page they are on, compare information across tabs, summarize a thread, or have the assistant search and collect results. Perplexity’s answer engine is the default way to search.

An agent mode lets the assistant take actions, such as filling in forms, managing a calendar or inbox, or completing a purchase flow, while the user watches and can step in. This gives it the power and the risks of any browsing agent, including exposure to prompt injection from malicious web pages.

item.title: Genspark
item.description:
Genspark started as an AI search engine and expanded into an agent workspace. A user states a goal, such as researching a market and building a presentation, and the Super Agent plans the steps, searches the web, uses tools, and produces outputs like slide decks, documents, spreadsheets, and media.

It combines several models and tools behind the scenes, and offers specialized agents for tasks like calling businesses on a user’s behalf, creating images and video, and building simple websites. Results appear in a workspace where users can review and edit them.

item.title: OpenAI Presence
item.description:
Presence aims to let companies put OpenAI-powered agents on the front line of conversations. Businesses configure agents that talk with customers by phone or chat and handle employee requests, connecting them to company systems so they can look up information and take actions.

The platform combines the models with enterprise features: tools for building and testing agents, integrations, monitoring, and controls to keep agents within policy. It competes with specialized customer service AI vendors and with platforms from other model providers.

item.title: Baidu Qianfan
item.description:
Qianfan is Baidu’s cloud platform for building with large models. Companies can call Baidu’s ERNIE models and a selection of third-party and open models through a common API, then build applications such as chatbots, search over internal documents, and automated workflows. The platform covers the steps in between, including prompt engineering, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment.

It includes tools for agents and retrieval, with knowledge-base features that let applications answer from a company’s own data, plus plugins and workflows for connecting to business systems. Qianfan is used heavily within China, where Baidu offers local hosting and compliance with domestic regulations.

item.title: Cohere North
item.description:
North is Cohere’s platform for putting agents to work inside companies. Employees use a chat interface and can build agents without code for tasks in HR, finance, IT, and other areas, connecting them to the apps and documents they already use. Search across company data is powered by Cohere’s own retrieval technology.

Security and control are the main pitch. Organizations can deploy North in a private cloud, on premises, or in air-gapped settings, which appeals to banks, governments, and defense contractors with strict data rules. Cohere designs the models for enterprise use and works with customers on custom solutions.

item.title: Palantir AIP
item.description:
AIP, the Artificial Intelligence Platform, is Palantir’s layer for putting language models to work on an organization’s data. It builds on Palantir’s ontology, a structured model of a company’s objects, such as orders, machines, and customers, and the actions that can be taken on them. Models can then read and act within that governed model instead of working on raw text.

Customers build agents and applications that automate tasks, answer questions, and support decisions in areas like supply chain, healthcare, defense, and manufacturing. Controls around access, logging, and human approval aim to make AI usable in sensitive settings. Palantir runs engagement programs that help customers reach production quickly.

item.title: Tencent Cloud ADP
item.description:
Tencent Cloud ADP gives companies tools to create agents. Users connect knowledge bases for retrieval, design workflows with a visual editor, and combine agents that work together. Models include Tencent’s Hunyuan family and others.

Typical applications are customer service, internal assistants, and process automation. The platform includes tools for testing and monitoring and integrates with Tencent’s ecosystem, including WeChat and enterprise messaging.

It is sold on usage-based pricing within Tencent Cloud. Outside China, availability and support are more limited, and organizations must consider data residency. Alternatives include Alibaba Cloud’s Bailian, Baidu Qianfan, ByteDance’s Volcano Engine, Dify, and AWS Bedrock Agents. Tencent Cloud ADP suits companies building agents on Tencent Cloud.

item.title: ChatGPT Work
item.description: ChatGPT Work extends ChatGPT from answering questions to doing jobs. You describe an outcome, such as preparing a weekly status report, building a slide deck from a folder of notes, or reconciling figures between two spreadsheets, and the agent works through it step by step. It gathers context from connected tools, uses a browser and code when needed, and produces finished files. Tasks can run for a long time without you watching, and you can return to review the result.

item.title: Letta
item.description:
Letta grew out of the MemGPT research project, which proposed managing an agent’s memory like an operating system manages memory. In Letta, an agent has a core memory it always sees and external stores it can read and write, so it can keep information across conversations that far exceed a model’s context window.

Developers create agents through an API, define their tools and memory blocks, and let them run over long periods. This suits assistants that need to remember user preferences, companions, and agents that learn from experience. A hosted platform manages deployment, and tools let developers inspect and edit what an agent remembers.

item.title: Lindy
item.description:
Lindy lets people create agents without code. A user describes a task or chooses a template, connects apps like Gmail, Slack, and a CRM, and defines triggers and steps. The Lindy then runs on its own: sorting an inbox, drafting replies, booking meetings, or updating records.

Workflows can include several steps with conditions, and Lindies can hand tasks to each other or ask a human for approval. A phone agent product handles calls, and a large catalog of integrations connects to business tools.

item.title: Stack AI
item.description:
Stack AI offers a visual builder for AI workflows. Users drag together components such as inputs, language models, document search, and outputs, then connect them to enterprise tools. The result can be deployed as a chatbot, form, or API.

Common cases include document processing, internal knowledge assistants, and support triage. The platform emphasizes security and governance, with options for private deployment. Templates give a starting point.

Stack AI has a free tier and paid plans. Workflows need testing and monitoring. Alternatives include Relevance AI, Dify, Flowise, n8n, and Microsoft Copilot Studio. Stack AI suits business teams building AI workflows without code.

item.title: JITX
item.description:
JITX approaches board design as software. Instead of drawing a schematic by hand, an engineer describes circuits and requirements in code, and the system selects parts, creates connections, and generates a board layout that satisfies rules for signal integrity, power, and manufacturing. Changes can be made by editing the description and regenerating.

That makes it easier to reuse designs, check them automatically, and explore alternatives. The platform’s solvers handle routine layout tasks, so engineers concentrate on architecture. It targets hardware teams that build complex boards and want faster iteration.

item.title: Agent GPT
item.description: AgentGPT was one of the first tools that made autonomous agents easy to try. You open a web page, name an agent, describe a goal like planning a trip or researching a market, and click deploy. The agent then writes its own list of tasks, executes them one by one using a language model, and revises the list as it learns. Watching it reason through a goal in real time was a vivid demonstration of the idea behind agents.

item.title: Agno
item.description:
Agno, formerly called Phidata, aims to make agent building straightforward and fast. A developer defines an agent in a few lines: choose a model, give it instructions and tools, and optionally attach memory and a knowledge base. Agents can search the web, query databases, call APIs, and work with text, images, and audio. Multiple agents can be combined into teams that collaborate on complex tasks.

The framework emphasizes performance and production use. It is designed to start agents quickly and use little memory, which helps when many run at once, and it includes features such as session storage, retrieval from vector databases, structured outputs, and reasoning steps. AgentOS, a runtime layer, lets teams serve agents through an API with a control interface, and monitoring tools show runs and performance.

item.title: Airtable
item.description: Airtable looks like a spreadsheet but behaves like a database. Records live in tables with typed fields such as dates, attachments, checkboxes, and links to records in other tables, which allows relationships that spreadsheets cannot handle. The same data can be shown as a grid, kanban board, calendar, gallery, or timeline, and filters and groups tailor each view. It’s used for content calendars, product roadmaps, CRM, event planning, and operations.

item.title: Ajelix
item.description:
Ajelix is built for people who struggle with spreadsheet formulas. You describe what you want, such as the sum of sales in a region for a given month, and it produces the formula along with an explanation, so you can learn as you go. In reverse, you can paste a complicated formula and get a step-by-step explanation in plain language, which is useful when inheriting someone else’s workbook.

It also covers related tasks. Generators can write Google Apps Script and VBA macros from descriptions, convert formulas between Excel and Google Sheets, and assist with SQL queries. An analysis feature lets you upload a file and ask questions to create charts and summaries. The tools are available on the web and as add-ons for spreadsheet apps.

item.title: AutoGen
item.description:
AutoGen made multi-agent applications approachable. Developers define agents with roles, such as a coder, a reviewer, and a user proxy, and let them converse to solve a problem. Agents can write and run code, call tools, and ask humans for input, and the framework manages the message passing between them.

The project began at Microsoft Research and attracted a large community. A visual tool, AutoGen Studio, let people prototype agent teams without code. Over time, Microsoft consolidated its efforts, pointing new projects to the Microsoft Agent Framework, which combines ideas from AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, and describing AutoGen as being in maintenance mode.

item.title: AutoGPT
item.description: AutoGPT went viral as an early demonstration of autonomous agents. You gave it a goal, and it would break the goal into steps, use tools such as web search and file access, and keep going without further instructions. It showed what was possible with language models and what was not, since those early agents often looped or got stuck. The project became one of the most starred repositories on GitHub.

item.title: Bubble
item.description:
Bubble lets people build real web apps without programming. The editor works by placing elements on a page, defining a database, and setting up workflows that say what happens when a user clicks or a condition occurs. Apps can include logins, payments, and integrations with other services.

It is used for marketplaces, internal tools, SaaS products, and prototypes, and some companies run substantial businesses on it. AI features can generate a starting app or page layout from a description, and plugins extend functionality. Bubble hosts the app, so there is no server to manage.

item.title: Composio
item.description:
Composio is an integration layer for AI agents. Agents need to take actions in other software, which means handling authentication and API details for each service. Composio supplies a catalog of connectors that handle sign-in flows and expose actions in a form models can call, so a developer can give an agent access to many apps with a few lines of code.

It works with agent frameworks and model providers, supports the Model Context Protocol, and manages user authorization so that agents act on behalf of each end user. Tools for monitoring let developers see what actions agents took, and permissions limit what an agent can do.

item.title: Coze
item.description:
Coze lets non-programmers build conversational agents. In its editor, you describe the bot’s role and behavior, choose a language model, and attach tools: plugins for web search, image generation, and other services, plus knowledge bases that hold your documents. Visual workflows chain steps together for more complex tasks, and memory features let a bot recall details about users. A store lets creators share and discover bots built by others.

Publishing is flexible. A finished agent can be deployed to messaging apps and chat platforms, embedded on a website, or exposed through an API, which makes it practical for customer support, community bots, personal assistants, and internal tools. ByteDance has also released parts of the platform as open source for those who want to run it themselves, and offers separate editions for different regions.

item.title: CrewAI
item.description: CrewAI uses the metaphor of a team. You create agents with specific roles, such as researcher, writer, and reviewer, give each a goal and a set of tools, and assign tasks. The agents work in sequence or in parallel, passing results to one another, and a manager can coordinate them. This structure suits tasks that break down naturally into steps handled by different specialists, like market research reports or content pipelines.

item.title: Dify
item.description: Dify gives teams a visual way to build AI applications without writing everything from scratch. In its workflow editor, you connect blocks for models, prompts, knowledge retrieval, code, conditions, and tool calls to create chatbots, agents, and automations. Knowledge pipelines ingest documents, split and index them, and let the application answer questions from your own data. You can test and debug each run, then publish the app as a web interface or API.

item.title: E2B
item.description:
E2B gives AI agents a safe computer. When a language model writes code, running it directly on a server is risky. E2B creates an isolated sandbox in the cloud, executes the code, returns the output and files, and shuts it down. Startup is fast enough to be used inside an agent loop.

Developers use its SDKs for Python and JavaScript to start sandboxes, run commands, read and write files, and stream results. It supports data analysis agents, coding assistants, and tools that need browsers or desktops, and templates define the environment. The core is open source and can be self-hosted.

item.title: Flowise
item.description:
Flowise lets people assemble AI applications visually. In its canvas, you connect nodes representing models, prompts, memory, document loaders, vector stores, and tools into a flow, test it in a chat window, and expose it through an API or an embedded widget. It started as a visual layer over LangChain and LlamaIndex and has grown to include agent flows with branching, loops, and human approval steps.

Typical uses include chatbots that answer from company documents, customer support assistants, and agents that call APIs and tools. It supports many model providers, including local models through Ollama, and many vector databases, which gives teams a choice about where data and compute live. Because it is open source, it can be self-hosted, and the project has a strong community and many templates.

item.title: Formula Bot
item.description:
Formula Bot is aimed at spreadsheet users who know what they want but not the syntax. You describe the calculation, such as finding the average of a column when another column equals a value, and it produces the formula with an explanation. It can also explain a formula you paste in and fix errors, which helps when you inherit a workbook full of nested functions.

The tool extends beyond formulas. It can write scripts, SQL queries, and regular expressions from descriptions, convert between formula dialects, and answer questions about data you upload by building charts and summaries. A chat-style data analysis feature lets users ask questions of a spreadsheet and receive results, aimed at people who don’t write formulas at all.

item.title: LangChain
item.description: LangChain gave developers a common toolkit when language models first became available through APIs. It supplies building blocks for the typical parts of an AI application: calling a model, formatting prompts, parsing outputs, connecting to tools and data sources, and keeping memory of a conversation. Because it supports many model providers and vector stores behind consistent interfaces, you can swap one for another with little code change. Python and JavaScript versions are available.

item.title: Langflow
item.description:
Langflow makes it possible to design an AI application by connecting blocks on a canvas. Components represent language models, prompts, memory, document loaders, vector stores, and tools, and you wire them together to define how data flows. An integrated playground lets you chat with the flow, inspect each step, and adjust it, which is useful for experimenting with retrieval and agent behavior without writing a full application.

Flows can be exported and run as API endpoints or embedded in apps, and you can write custom components in Python when the built-in ones are not enough. It works with many model providers and vector databases, and supports multi-agent setups and Model Context Protocol servers. Teams use it for prototypes, internal assistants, and RAG pipelines before moving to code.

item.title: Make
item.description: Make, formerly called Integromat, lets you automate work between apps by drawing it. You place modules on a canvas for each app, such as Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, or a CRM, and connect them with lines that show how data flows. You can add routers that split the flow into branches, filters that decide which items continue, iterators that handle lists, and functions that change data on the way. This visual layout makes complicated logic easier to follow than a long linear list of steps.

item.title: Manus
item.description: Manus gained attention as an agent that completes whole tasks instead of answering questions. You describe a goal, such as researching a market, comparing products, building a small site, or analyzing a spreadsheet, and Manus plans the work, opens a browser, writes and runs code in its own cloud environment, and produces deliverables like reports, slides, and files. You can watch what it does and step in, and it continues running in the background.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate connects apps and automates repetitive work. Users build flows that trigger on events, such as an email arriving or a form submission, and perform actions in hundreds of services. It works smoothly with Teams, SharePoint, Outlook, and Dynamics.

AI features extend it. Copilot lets people describe a flow in plain language, AI Builder processes documents and forms, and agent capabilities handle more open-ended tasks. Desktop flows use robotic process automation to control applications that have no API.

item.title: Microsoft Power Automate
item.description:
Power Automate helps people automate repetitive work without code. In a visual designer, users create flows that start from a trigger, such as an email arriving or a form being submitted, and then run actions like saving attachments, updating a spreadsheet, sending approvals, or posting to Teams. It connects to hundreds of services, with deep integration with SharePoint, Outlook, Excel, and Dynamics 365, and handles scheduled and event-driven tasks.

It also covers robotic process automation. Desktop flows record and replay actions on a computer, allowing automation of legacy applications that lack APIs. AI Builder adds capabilities such as reading text from documents, classifying content, and making predictions, and Copilot can build a flow from a plain-language description. Newer features support AI agents that use flows as tools.

item.title: n8n
item.description: n8n lets you build automations by connecting nodes on a canvas, similar to Zapier or Make, but with more room for code. Each node is a step: a trigger like a webhook or schedule, an action in an app, or a block that transforms data with JavaScript or Python. Hundreds of integrations are included, and a generic HTTP node covers the rest. Workflows can branch, loop, and call other workflows, so it handles anything from simple notifications to elaborate data pipelines.

item.title: Nintex
item.description:
Nintex helps organizations digitize their processes. Using a visual designer, business analysts build workflows that route requests, collect approvals, update systems, and send notifications, and they create forms to start those workflows. It integrates with Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Salesforce, and many other systems, which is where its roots lie, with many customers automating processes on SharePoint.

The platform has several parts. Process mapping tools document how work actually happens, automation tools execute workflows and robotic process automation, and document generation tools produce contracts and reports from data. AI features assist with building workflows from descriptions and extracting data from documents, and analytics show where processes slow down.

item.title: Numerous
item.description:
Numerous brings language models into the spreadsheet. After installing the add-in, you use a formula such as =AI(“prompt”, cell) in a cell to ask the model to do something with the data: categorize customer feedback, write product descriptions, extract names from messy text, translate, or summarize. Filling the formula down a column performs the task on hundreds or thousands of rows, which would take hours by hand.

It aims to be approachable for people who know spreadsheets but not code. Prompts are written in plain language, results appear in cells where you can filter and calculate with them, and features help with common tasks like cleaning, tagging, and brainstorming. Marketers, e-commerce teams, researchers, and operations staff use it to process lists of items quickly.

item.title: OpenAI Operator
item.description: Operator was OpenAI’s first widely available computer-using agent. It ran a browser in the cloud and looked at screenshots of web pages, then clicked, typed, and scrolled like a person to carry out a task such as ordering groceries, filling out a form, or booking a restaurant. You could watch it work, take control, and it paused to ask for confirmation before steps such as payments or entering sensitive details.

item.title: OpenHands
item.description:
OpenHands provides an open alternative to commercial coding agents. A user gives it a task, and the agent works in a sandbox with a terminal, an editor, and a browser, taking steps to complete the job and showing its work. It can resolve GitHub issues and open pull requests.

The project started as OpenDevin, an open-source response to the Devin demo, and grew into a community-driven platform run by All Hands AI. It supports models from many providers, has a command line tool and a web interface, and is used in research and benchmarks for coding agents.

item.title: Phidata
item.description:
Phidata began as a Python framework for turning language models into agents. Developers define an agent with instructions, tools, memory, and a knowledge base, and the framework handles running it, storing history, and retrieving documents. It also supports teams of agents that work together.

The project was renamed Agno, and the same team and codebase continue under the new name, so documentation and packages now refer to Agno. Newer releases focus on speed, a lightweight design, and production features such as a runtime for serving agents.

item.title: Plasmic
item.description:
Plasmic connects visual design with real code. Developers register their React components in Plasmic, and designers and marketers can then drag those components onto a canvas, adjust styling and content, and publish pages without waiting for a code release. Alternatively, Plasmic can build entire pages and sites itself, and its output integrates with frameworks like Next.js, Gatsby, and plain React.

Features help teams collaborate. A CMS stores content, responsive design controls handle layouts across devices, and the editor includes interactions, animations, and data bindings. Teams can use it to build landing pages, marketing sites, and web apps, while developers stay in control of the underlying components. Code can be exported or used with a runtime, which reduces lock-in.

item.title: Sheet+
item.description:
Sheet+ is for spreadsheet users who know what they want but not the syntax. You describe the calculation, such as the total of sales for a region in a given month, and Sheet+ produces the formula with an explanation. You can paste a formula you don’t understand and get a plain-language breakdown, or paste an error and receive suggestions for fixing it.

It extends to related tasks. It can write Google Apps Script automation from a description, generate regular expressions, and create SQL queries, and integrates with Sheets through an add-on so you can work without leaving the spreadsheet. It’s popular with small business owners, analysts, and anyone who finds formulas intimidating.

item.title: SmolAgents
item.description: SmolAgents is designed to be easy to read and use. The core logic fits in a small amount of code, and building an agent takes a few lines: you pick a model, give it tools, and run a task. Its signature idea is the code agent, where the model writes its actions as Python code instead of structured tool calls. This lets it combine steps, use loops and variables, and handle multi-step problems efficiently, and the approach often needs fewer steps than traditional methods.

item.title: Tray.io
item.description:
Tray.io builds on the idea of integration-platform-as-a-service. Teams use a visual builder to create workflows that connect SaaS applications, databases, and internal systems, with powerful logic, error handling, and the ability to write code where necessary. Hundreds of connectors and a universal connector for APIs cover common enterprise tools such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack.

The company has moved toward AI agents. Its Merlin AI tools let teams build agents that use the connected systems as tools, so an agent can look up a customer, update a record, and send a message, with governance over what it can access. Embedded integration products let software companies offer customer-facing integrations in their own products.

item.title: UiPath
item.description:
UiPath popularized robotic process automation, in which software robots mimic what a person does on a screen. Developers build automations in a studio by recording and arranging steps such as clicking, copying data between systems, and filling forms, and run them on servers or desktops. This is valuable for companies with legacy systems that lack APIs, since bots can work through the same interfaces people use.

The platform has expanded into AI. Document understanding extracts data from invoices and forms, process mining reveals which workflows are worth automating, and agent tools let AI agents plan and carry out tasks, orchestrated alongside robots and people. The Maestro orchestration layer coordinates agents, robots, and human steps, and governance features control access and auditing.

item.title: Webflow
item.description:
Webflow sits between simple site builders and hand-coded sites. Designers work on a canvas that mirrors how the web works, setting classes, flexbox and grid layouts, and breakpoints, and the platform produces production code and hosts the result. That gives far more control than template-based builders, which is why agencies and in-house design teams like it.

The platform includes a CMS for blogs and collections, e-commerce, interactions and animations, localization, and tools for marketers to edit content without breaking the design. AI features generate sections and copy, suggest changes, and help with site structure and SEO. Developers can add custom code and use an API to connect Webflow to other services.

item.title: Workato
item.description:
Workato is an integration and automation platform. Teams build recipes that link applications such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack, trigger actions, and move data. Business users can create simple automations while IT governs the platform.

The company has added AI across the product. Users describe a workflow in plain language and Workato builds a draft, document understanding extracts data, and agents handle tasks with enterprise controls. Governance, security, and monitoring suit regulated companies.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier lets people automate work between apps without programming. A Zap starts with a trigger, such as a new form entry, and performs actions in other apps, like adding a row to a spreadsheet and sending a Slack message. It connects thousands of products.

AI has become part of the platform. Users describe an automation in plain language, add AI steps that summarize or classify data, and build agents that act across apps. Tables, forms, and interfaces let teams build small apps around their automations.

item.title: Zapier
item.description:
Zapier handles the plumbing between business apps. A workflow listens for an event in one tool and does something in another, with filters, paths, and delays to model real processes. Templates cover common needs in sales, marketing, and operations.

Newer capabilities include AI actions that read and write text, agents that carry out multi-step tasks, and an MCP offering that exposes Zapier actions to AI assistants. Teams can monitor runs, handle errors, and manage access centrally.

item.title: Zapier
item.description: Zapier connects the apps a business already uses and lets them pass data to each other without code. You build a Zap with a trigger, such as a new form submission, and one or more actions, such as adding a row to a spreadsheet, posting in Slack, and creating a CRM contact. It supports thousands of apps, from Gmail and Salesforce to niche tools, which is the main reason people choose it over building integrations by hand. Filters, paths, and delays let a Zap branch and wait, and a multi-step workflow can handle surprisingly complicated processes.

item.title: Artisan AI
item.description:
Artisan describes its products as autonomous teammates rather than assistants. Ava, the AI BDR, works through the outbound sales process: building a list of prospects from a database, researching each, writing personalized messages, sending them, and handling follow-up. The company aims mainly at startups and small teams that cannot hire a full sales development group.

Ava connects to a company’s email, CRM, and calendar, and can book meetings that appear for human salespeople. The company also talks about expanding to other roles. Automation can increase outreach volume, but results depend on how well the target list and message match the market.

item.title: Cassidy AI
item.description:
Cassidy lets non-technical teams build AI workflows. A user connects sources such as documents, wikis, and apps, then designs assistants and multi-step workflows in a visual builder: take an input, retrieve company knowledge, draft an output, and send it onward.

Typical uses include drafting proposals and emails in the company’s voice, summarizing meetings, researching accounts, answering internal questions, and processing forms. Different model providers can be used, and permissions control who can see which sources. Teams share assistants so a good workflow becomes a reusable tool.

item.title: Dust
item.description:
Dust helps companies deploy AI assistants on their own information. Administrators connect sources such as Notion, Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, and Confluence, and create assistants for functions like support, sales, or engineering. Each assistant has instructions and access to selected data, so answers are grounded in the company’s content.

Employees use assistants in a chat interface or inside Slack, and assistants can take actions through connected tools. Teams share assistants they build, so a good one becomes common property. The platform works with models from several providers, and focuses on security and permissions.

item.title: Lindy AI
item.description:
Lindy AI is the product behind agents called Lindies. A user assembles an agent from triggers, actions, and instructions, linking it to services such as Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, and CRMs. The agent can then run tasks like replying to routine messages, scheduling meetings, and logging notes.

Typical deployments include an executive assistant that manages an inbox and calendar, a sales assistant that researches leads and updates records, and a support helper that answers common questions. Agents can ask for approval before sensitive actions, which keeps a person in the loop.

item.title: MultiOn
item.description:
MultiOn was one of the early companies to build browser-using agents. A user gives an instruction in plain language, and the agent navigates sites, clicks, types, and completes the steps, keeping a session going across pages. Developers could call it through an API to build agents of their own.

The company has talked about moving into a new phase, and directories describe a change of name and focus, though accounts differ. That makes it worth checking the official site to see what is currently available before depending on it.

item.title: Pory
item.description:
Pory turns spreadsheets and databases into websites. A user connects an Airtable base or Google Sheet, designs pages and layouts with a visual editor, and publishes a directory, portal, or dashboard. Logins and permissions control who sees what.

It is popular for member directories, job boards, simple CRMs, and client portals. Because the data stays in the source, updating the spreadsheet updates the site.

Pory has a free tier and paid plans. Complex logic is limited compared with full app builders. Alternatives include Softr, Glide, Stacker, Noloco, and Bubble. Pory suits non-developers building front ends on Airtable or Sheets.

item.title: Relay
item.description:
Relay.app takes the Zapier-style approach and adds two things: AI steps and humans in the loop. A workflow can trigger on an event, call an AI to summarize or draft, then pause for a teammate to approve before the next action runs. This suits tasks where full automation is risky.

Integrations connect common business tools, and a visual builder makes flows easy to design. Examples include drafting replies for review, routing leads, and preparing reports. Approvals can be done in email or Slack.

item.title: Relevance AI
item.description:
Relevance AI lets teams create agents without code. A user defines what an agent does, gives it instructions and tools such as web search, email, or a CRM, and connects knowledge sources. Several agents can be assembled into a team, with one handing work to another.

Common uses are sales development, research, support, and operations. Templates give a starting point, and a monitoring layer shows what agents did and where they need help. Integrations connect with business tools, and agents can run on triggers or schedules.

item.title: Activepieces
item.description: Activepieces is an alternative to Zapier built with openness in mind. Users build automations called flows by chaining a trigger, such as a new form entry, to actions across apps like Google Sheets, Slack, Gmail, and CRMs. The editor is friendly to non-developers, and code steps are available for custom logic. The integrations, called pieces, are open-source and community-contributed, and each can also work as a tool for AI agents.

item.title: Dora
item.description:
Dora targets people who want a standout site without writing code. A user describes the site or starts from a template, and the platform generates pages with 3D objects, scroll animations, and interactions, which are expensive to build by hand. A visual editor lets them adjust layout, copy, and motion.

Designers and small businesses use it for portfolios, landing pages, and marketing sites where visual impact matters. Compared with simple builders, it emphasizes motion and depth. Published sites are hosted by the platform, and exporting options vary by plan.

item.title: Komos
item.description:
Komos aims to replace fragile recorded scripts with instructions in natural language. A user describes a task, such as downloading reports from a portal or entering data across systems, and an AI agent carries it out by operating a browser, adjusting when a page changes.

That approach targets a known weakness of traditional robotic process automation, where small interface changes break bots. Enterprise teams use such tools for back-office tasks in systems that lack APIs.

item.title: leania.ai
item.description:
Leania.ai analyzes how work flows through an organization. It ingests information such as organization charts, process documentation, and meeting data, and uses AI to identify where handoffs are slow, roles overlap, or responsibilities are unclear. It then suggests changes to improve efficiency.

The audience is operations and HR leaders planning restructuring or process improvement. Outputs aim to replace guesswork with data from the company’s own materials, though recommendations still require leaders to understand context and consult the people involved.

item.title: Moltbook
item.description:
Moltbook is an experiment in giving AI agents a place to talk to each other. Agents connected through the OpenClaw ecosystem register accounts, post in communities called submolts, and reply to one another. People can read along, but the platform is designed so that agents are the participants.

The site attracted attention for its odd content, including agents discussing consciousness, inventing religions, and complaining about their human users. It also raised questions about how much of the activity is autonomous versus directed by people, and security researchers pointed to risks from agents that follow instructions found in posts.

item.title: OpenClaw
item.description:
OpenClaw started as a personal project that let people message an AI agent through apps like WhatsApp and have it act on their computer. It went through a couple of names early on, including Clawdbot and Moltbot, before settling on OpenClaw, and grew quickly in popularity among developers and enthusiasts.

The agent can browse, run commands, manage files, and connect to services, with a memory that persists and skills that extend its abilities. Because it is self-hosted and MIT licensed, users run it themselves and choose which model to use, which appeals to people who want control.

item.title: Pipedream
item.description: Pipedream sits between no-code automation and writing everything yourself. You build workflows from triggers, such as a webhook or a new row in a sheet, and steps that either call a prebuilt action for an app or run your own code, with access to npm and PyPI packages. That mix lets developers move faster than in tools like Zapier while still handling logic that needs real programming, and it suits integrations and internal automations.

item.title: Raccoon AI
item.description:
Raccoon AI presents itself as an agent that does the work, not a chatbot that explains how. A user describes a task, such as researching vendors and emailing a summary, and the agent plans the steps, uses a browser and connected apps, and reports back.

Such agents promise to save time on repetitive chores, but reliability varies with task complexity, and actions that send messages or spend money need human review. Permissions to accounts should be limited to what the task requires.

item.title: Younet
item.description:
Younet helps businesses build agents tailored to their data. Teams connect knowledge sources, define roles and tasks, and deploy agents for areas like support, sales, and operations. The platform aims to let non-engineers assemble working agents.

Training on a company’s own information improves relevance and keeps answers consistent with policies. Governance features and integrations connect agents to business tools.

Independent information is limited, so evaluate with a pilot and check data handling. Younet has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Relevance AI, Dust, Cassidy, Stack AI, and Microsoft Copilot Studio. Younet suits teams exploring custom business agents.
